title: Internal memo reveals GOP panic as its greatest weapon backfires
content: While the Republican Party has made redistricting a key part of its political strategy — particularly after President Donald Trump demanded the gerrymandering of Texas last August — a new internal memo reveals that the GOP is worried that it will lose the upcoming round of redistricting battles in 2028, warning that the resulting map could deliver a “permanent Democratic House majority.” This is according to the conservative outlet the Washington Examiner , which on Wednesday reported on a memo entitled “Battle Beneath the Ballot,” in which the Republican State Leadership Committee argued that the party’s failure to invest in down-ballot state legislative elections could mean the decision to launch a redistricting war was a huge mistake. As the Examiner explains, the memo revealed that “Democrats’ four largest groups involved in state legislative elections will outspend the RSLC’s commitment of more than $50 million by almost three-to-one. Republicans have a huge fundraising lead nationally, with the likes of MAGA Inc., the Trump-aligned super PAC, holding a $400 million war chest. But all the signs are that it will be spent on congressional and gubernatorial races, rather than less glamorous down-ballot fights.” The Democrats, meanwhile, have a robust state-level plan.  According to the Examiner, “This year four major Democratic organizations have publicly announced significant spending plans: the Democratic Legislative Campaign Committee at $50 million, Forward Majority at $30 million, LCV Victory Fund at more than $50 million, and the National Democratic Redistricting Committee at $4 million. In all, they are committed to spending more than $134 million.” “This flood of national liberal dollars into state legislative races should concern everyone who does not want to see a permanent Democratic House majority,” warns the memo. While the RSLC asserts that more money should be spent at a state level “to ensure the best possible House battlefield in 2028 , it also points to the 2030 census, in which all 50 states will redraw their voting maps. “If we are serious about preventing a permanent Democratic House majority,” the memo reiterates, “we must recognize that the fight for Congress begins in state legislative districts, not in congressional campaigns,” explaining that a handful of seats will have a major impact on key districts. The Republican Party, says the memo, should focus its efforts on state legislatures in Michigan, Minnesota, Pennsylvania, and Wisconsin, as state senate wins would allow them to shape up to 12 House districts, potentially delivering a major boost to the GOP on a federal level. The report comes as polling shows Republicans face major headwinds going into the midterms, in which the party is projected to lose its majority in the House and possibly the Senate. Surveys have found that on a generic ballot, Democrats have their strongest lead in polling history.

title: Alabama AG Marshall fires back at USPS mail-ballot order critics: ‘This is about securing elections’
content: Republican Alabama Attorney General Steve Marshall argues that his Democratic counterparts do not care about election integrity in the same way Republicans do, as they attempt to block measures designed to root out illegal voters they have long claimed do not exist. Marshall addressed a legal challenge brought by 25 Democratic state attorneys general challenging President Donald Trump's executive order that included provisions for federal agencies to help states ensure only citizens receive mail-in ballots, and for the U.S. Postal Service to institute practices to make the ballots trackable. "The left, because they’re concerned about losing at the midterms, want to be able to obstruct this administration’s efforts to ensure the integrity of our elections," Marshall told Fox News Digital this week, ahead of Thursday's oral arguments before U.S. District Judge Indira Talwani in Boston. "You have to wonder – when those that are objecting to this – how confident they can be in the security of their elections, as opposed to becoming just a partisan opportunity to ensure the Democrats win and keep conservative voices from being heard, not only in local and state levels of government, but particularly in Washington." DHS PLANS COSTLY CRACKDOWN ON STATES THAT DON’T COOPERATE ON ELECTION SECURITY Marshall led a letter in July from 13 Republican attorneys general, backing the U.S. Postal Service's following up on Trump's March 31 executive order that set up an audit of states' voter rolls . "There shouldn't be a reason why we object to that, but yet Democrats simply don't want to have fair elections in a way that people can have confidence," Marshall claimed. Fox News Digital reached out to the Democratic Attorneys General Association for comment on Marshall's remarks, but they did not immediately respond. Democrats, in various arguments to block the audit of voter rolls before the mailing out of absentee ballots, claim that it would lead to "disenfranchisement," "chaos," "unconstitutional overreach" and a partisan "power grab." Democrats' concern is that if they refuse to share their voter rolls with the Department of Homeland Security and Social Security Administration to crosscheck the eligibility of legal voters, the USPS can stop the mailing of state's absentee ballots. "USPS's interest in correcting an unsubstantiated problem through likely unconstitutional means is dwarfed by the overwhelming risk of pervasive disenfranchisement of citizens who need access to mail ballots in order to vote," Talwani, appointed by former President Barack Obama, wrote in her restraining order against the Trump administration. FEDERAL JUDGE BLOCKS TRUMP ADMINISTRATION FROM RESTRICTING MAIL-IN BALLOTS AHEAD OF MIDTERMS "The postal service is not a partisan organization. As the postmaster said, I think most recently, we're just there to deliver the mail. They're experts in how it is that this can be configured." Marshall stated that the problem of voter fraud is documented, not "unsubstantiated," as Talwani put it, with evidence in his own state. USPS WOULDN'T DELIVER BALLOTS IN STATES THAT REFUSE TO FORK OVER MAIL-IN VOTER INFO UNDER PROPOSED RULE "This is not a solution looking for a problem," he said. "This is in response to what we know is going on across the country. And this provides a commonsense, straightforward way for states to be able to ensure elections, but most importantly, for the people of this country to have belief that their elections in fact are accurate." MAIL-VOTING CRACKDOWN MOVES AHEAD AS TRUMP COURT WIN OPENS DOOR TO FEDERAL ACTION "It's not a shock that Democrats are standing up the ability for us to pass the SAVE [America] Act because they don't want to allow for there to be assurances of what is already in the law: That somebody here illegally cannot be able to vote," he added. "But here we have the president being able to make sure that we are allowing for government resources to be used in an appropriate way to simply allow those who are qualified to vote, vote, and those who aren't, don't." Marshall has little confidence that the Obama-appointed judge in Boston is going to side with the Trump administration and the law. "I would be remiss if I didn't say that I would fully expect her to continue with the Democratic Party line," he said. "The Trump administration has already filed a request with the First Circuit to try to get a stay of that order, but yet we're going to continue to battle this case along with the administration and look forward to standing beside them when they obtain this victory." TRUMP SCORES SUPREME COURT WIN ON MAIL-IN VOTING RESTRICTIONS BEFORE MIDTERMS Marshall maintains Republicans are not stopping anyone from getting an absentee ballot – they're just trying to make sure the process is conducted legally and securely. "Here we have a barcode that allows us to be able to connect it directly with the voter – we have the assurance that that ballot is being cast by the person in fact that receives that ballot," he said. "Democrats and Republicans alike ought to praise this as a commonsense effort to be able to restore election integrity in this area, but it's not a shock that Democrats have opposed it." MORE THAN A QUARTER-MILLION NONCITIZENS MAY BE REGISTERED TO VOTE IN 4 KEY STATES, DHS ALLEGES Marhall pointed to the 2005 bipartisan commission chaired by former President Jimmy Carter and former Secretary of State James Baker that identified mailed absentee ballots as being susceptible to fraud. "This is about securing elections, not interfering with states' abilities to conduct elections, and we think that we'll be able to eliminate many of the issues that we've seen, including in Alabama, that have occurred in the past." The restraining order Talwani issued will remain in place for up to one more week while she considers whether to issue a longer-term preliminary injunction blocking the rule . The hearing is Thursday in Boston, but the fight will go on from states on both sides as the midterm mail-in ballot season officially gets underway.

title: Even MAGA Republicans say party is toast after seeing national Trump ad
content: President Donald Trump's political organization launched two national ads promoting himself and the administration as part of his effort to help Republicans win the 2026 midterm election. But even Republicans agree that if this is the way Trump intends to help, the GOP "is so screwed." New York Times reporter Teddy Schleifer posted the videos to X with comments about Trump being a "fighter" and an "inspiration." There's B-roll showing an American flag waving over a farm and a white family with two children holding hands. Footage shows Trump touring a company with men wearing hard hats and also several shots of Trump's new Air Force One plane that was a gift from Qatar. One video is from Trump's press conference showing off the plane, which is where "inspiration" appears across the screen. The second appears to show footage of a flyover by the Qatari plane in South Dakota. "And our top priority will be to create a nation that is proud, prosperous and free," Trump's voice is heard saying as the Statue of Liberty appears on screen. The second ad argues that Trump is making America more affordable with his "no tax on tips" policy up to $25,000. He celebrates his "no tax on overtime up to $12,500," and "no tax on Social Security" for those making less than $25,000 annually. Trump then cheers that he was able to reduce the price of eggs, which has dropped after the avian flu crisis ended in 2025. Other groceries remain up across the board as does fuel. Conservative Erick Erickson wasn't impressed by what he saw. "The GOP is so screwed in November if this is how the president spends his money," he wrote on X. One of the "Pod Save America" hosts, Dan Pfeiffer, similarly pointed to the ad's obvious flaws. "Not a single mention of anything Trump has done to help anyone. This ad could not be more out of touch with the political moment." CNN commentator and old-school strategist David Axelrod commented , "Maybe they think this will animate their base and soften discontent but if the @GOP spends its money trying to assuage the @POTUS 's ego, they are going to crash and burn this fall." "Which GOP candidate is this supposed to help, again?" said former Republican Party chairman, Michael Steele . "Feels like a reelect ad on Earth 3 and it has nothing about why voters in 2026 should vote GOP. Did they make an ad simply persuade the guy who sits behind the Resolute desk? This also feels like an ad Grok would have made," said former MSNBC host Chuck Todd . "The first ad appears to be about boosting Trump's numbers more than helping any vulnerable Republicans win races," s aid Annie Karni, New York Times congressional correspondent. Freelancer Nick Field questioned the ad , noting, "This one doesn't even bother to claim one accomplishment." Todd said about the second ad, "This is a better effort by the Trump team but it still is using the party’s most unpopular person as the star of the ad." Here's the new ad from Trump's political operation — it's all about Trump. pic.twitter.com/7dRL5tHvsj — Teddy Schleifer (@teddyschleifer) September 2, 2026 And here's another pro-Trump ad from Securing American Greatness that began airing nationally today. pic.twitter.com/wY3eNpCZOv — Teddy Schleifer (@teddyschleifer) September 2, 2026

title: Social media erupts after DeSantis gives ‘Soros’ protester a piece of his mind: ‘Ain’t my first rodeo’
content: Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis set social media aflame Tuesday night after he did not hold back in his response to a disruption by a woman he accused of being paid by George Soros, yelling back at her that "this ain’t my first rodeo." DeSantis was touting Florida’s economy at a state GOP campaign event in Tampa when he was interrupted mid-sentence by a heckler. The governor did not hesitate in his response. "Hey, Soros isn't paying you enough because you're not very good at this," he said, pointing to the woman as security personnel approached her in the crowd. "You should try again," DeSantis continued as the crowd booed the heckler. Keeping with the Soros line , DeSantis piled on, "He needs to pay some better talent instead of having people like you show up. This ain't my first rodeo, lady. I've seen it all, and you ain't very good at it." BYRON DONALDS SHUTS DOWN BILL MAHER’S CLAIM ON GOP PRIMARY RACISM, SAYS 'FLORIDA IS A MERITOCRACY' After another heckler interrupted the event again that same evening, DeSantis shot back, "Let me just give you guys some advice: standing up and screaming is not effective. Okay?" "I've seen people try to do this over the years," he continued. "Some are more effective than others." "I remember I had Antifa charge me, and one of our FDLE [Florida Department of Law Enforcement] leveled them, and it was funny, and it was good." "But here's the deal," he leaned in. "I think Soros is tightening his wallet because the people he's paying are terrible at this." SOROS PROSECUTOR IN DANGER OF BEING REMOVED AFTER GRIEVING MOM’S DESPERATE ALARM: ‘CAN’T BELIEVE THIS’ "He used to hire people who were really good. Now they're just screeching, and it's almost like, I don't even know what it is. And so, listen, you should be respectful, you should listen. This is part of the civic process," he said. "But, if you're not going to do that, do a better job at protesting, please. Gosh." "THAT'S MY GOVERNOR!!" reacted conservative commentator Eric Daugherty on X, writing, "DeSantis just PUMMELED a leftist heckler who disrupted his speech tonight." Another popular conservative influencer who simply goes by the name Greg reacted, "Soros protester is re-thinking opening her mouth at the RPOF [Republican Party of Florida] Event. DeSantis with the takedown." Another X account, DeSantis Appreciation Society, wrote, "The Tribal Chief @RonDeSantis just bodied a Soros protester into next week at the RPOF event." "DeSantis is a legend. Absolutely obliterated a liberal heckler, lol. Best governor ever!" wrote another popular conservative account going by the name "American Nightmare." ANTIFA-LINKED SITES GO DARK AFTER STATE DEPARTMENT TERROR DESIGNATION OF TECH COLLECTIVE SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER In response, a spokesperson for the Soros family’s philanthropic group, the Open Society Foundations, directed Fox News Digital to a 2025 statement that said, "We do not pay people to protest or directly train or coordinate protestors." While the statement called nonviolent public protests "hallmarks of any vibrant society," the group said that "All Open Society grantees are required to comply with the law and we expect our grantees to uphold our shared commitment to human rights, dignity, and nonviolence." Under the Florida Constitution, DeSantis, who is serving his second consecutive term, is not eligible to seek another consecutive term as governor this year. During Tuesday's event, he endorsed a statewide slate of Republicans, including GOP gubernatorial nominee U.S. Rep. Byron Donalds. The event showcased Donalds as well as other Republican candidates, Attorney General James Uthmeier, Florida Chief Financial Officer Blaise Ingoglia and Agriculture Commissioner Wilton Simpson.

title: 12th annual San Francisco Chinatown's Night Out to be hosted at a different venue
content: The 12th annual San Francisco Chinatown’s Night Out will be celebrated on Sept. 9 at a new venue. The event is intended to introduce the community to the cops and their commanders assigned to the area. “Public safety works best when officers build strong relationships with the people they serve. When beat officers know the store owners on their block. When an officer stops to help a senior, and when public safety workers know the neighborhood, and know the people who they’re there to protect,” Mayor Daniel Lurie said. With Portsmouth Square still under construction, Willie “Woo Woo” Wong Playground Park will be the site of the annual Chinatown Night Out. Organizers say about 1,000 people usually show up, each gets a meal and a grab bag full of goodies. Willie “Woo Woo” Wong has become one of the default parks in the neighborhood for seniors and others as Portsmouth Square goes through a major renovation. For SFPD this year, there’s also a feeling of accomplishment because crime rates continue to fall across the city. “We are down 20% across the board in all crime categories. And that’s already on top of historic lows from last year as well, so, I’m really happy of that result,” San Francisco Police Chief Derrick Lew said. In 2025, the city experienced a 30% drop in crime. In 2026, some categories are also at historic lows, including car break ins, which are the lowest in 23 years. Chinatown Night Out is also an opportunity for public safety departments to connect with community members. Fire Chief Dean Crispen says they are working with seniors in the neighborhood. “To create a placard that folks can put on their refrigerator, so that when EMT’s and paramedics respond, there’s communication about the medical issues and the medications the folks are taking,” Crispen said. The event is free and everyone is invited to join.

title: Nearly 9 in 10 Americans report widespread government corruption after Trump's return
content: Data: Gallup ; Chart: Avery Lotz/Axios Americans' perceptions of government corruption have hit a 20-year high following President Trump's return to office, a new Gallup survey found. Why it matters: The results signal a deepening crisis of confidence in the federal government as trust in U.S. institutions already hovers near an all-time low. By the numbers: 89% of U.S. adults say government corruption is widespread, Gallup found . That's a 10-point increase from last year and well above the 72%–79% range between 2010 and 2025. Democrats are driving most of the rise, jumping to 91% this year after sitting at 76% during the first year of Trump's term. In 2024, when President Biden was still in office, 57% of Democrats said government corruption was widespread. About 90% of independents think corruption is widespread, up 12 points since 2024. Between the lines: Trump raked in more than $2.2 billion in the first year of his second term. In 2024, he reported making about $600 million. A substantial share of Trump's income comes from non-traditional business holdings, like his cryptocurrency business. He faced criticism after an investment firm tied to the United Arab Emirates bought almost half of his main crypto firm, prmopting accusations of potential foreign influence over U.S. policy. He's also making money from a new plan to offer early access to his Truth Social posts, which can move markets. Zoom out: Congressional lawmakers have repeatedly called out what they say are conflicts of interests. Rep. Jamie Raskin (D-Md.) released a report in November that concluded Trump and his family significantly benefitted from rolling back crypto regulations designed to protect Americans from fraud and scams. Democrats have also criticized the president for accepting lavish gifts, including a $400 million Qatari jet . It's also not just the president — congressional lawmakers have faced growing scrutiny for making head-turning sums trading stocks while in office. What they're saying: "President Trump has launched an all-out war on fraud across the entire federal government, holding criminals accountable and saving taxpayers billions of dollars," White House spokesman Davis Ingle said in an emailed statement. "The Democrats in Congress have refused to do anything to stop waste, fraud, and abuse in our government." Zoom in: Republicans have held a much steadier view of government corruption. About eight in 10 say corruption is widespread, relatively on par with 2024 levels, when 87% said the same. Republicans' consistent reading suggests this feeling is widespread regardless of which political party is in power. The big picture: While citizens in many developed nations feel their governments are becoming less corrupt, Americans are experiencing the exact opposite trend. Among the 38 member countries in the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development, the median level of perceived government corruption has fallen from 69% in 2009 to below 60% since 2022. For the first time ever, the U.S. now tops perceived corruption ratings by comparison to the other countries in the OECD. Since 2023, just four other countries that Gallup has surveyed have scored higher than the U.S., including Lebanon, Peru, Ghana and Nigeria. The data for 2026 isn't complete because Gallup conducts their polling on a country-by-country basis over the year, so that massive gap could grow wider this year. Methodology: Gallup surveyed at least 1,000 Americans every year since 2005 to reach these results. It also surveyed between 500 and more than 3,000 people in other countries to measure sentiment across the other OECD countries. title: The MAGA Right Is Only Pretending to Be Censored
content: Updated at 7:41 a.m. ET on September 3, 2026 For nearly a year and a half, the Trump administration prepared its case. Political appointees inside the State Department combed through old files and databases. Civil servants received notice that their personal emails would be examined. Darren Beattie—the founder of a far-right conspiracist website, then the undersecretary of state for public diplomacy—sent out a request for files on anyone who had communicated with or written about the Global Engagement Center, a now-dissolved agency that once worked to expose propaganda campaigns by Russia, China, Iran, and other countries around the world. [ Read: The white nationalist in charge of Trump’s public diplomacy ] The request, seen last year by the MIT Technology Review , was far-reaching. Beattie was seeking information on Bill Gates; the commentator Bill Kristol; Chris Krebs, a former U.S. cybersecurity official; a German government minister; the analyst Renée DiResta, formerly at Stanford University, as well as others associated with a research project called the Election Integrity Partnership; and, as it happens, me. This unprecedented investigation was meant to expose the Biden administration’s “censorship–industrial complex,” a shadowy network allegedly dedicated to the mass suppression of American free speech. Since 2020, internet trolls have accused Biden-administration officials, social-media companies, and university researchers of weaving a nefarious plot to censor conservatives. Since 2025, MAGA ideologues have been using this alleged plot as an excuse to dismantle government programs, stifle research, intimidate American citizens, and even distort American foreign policy. And yet for the past year and half, neither Beattie nor anyone else has actually managed to prove that the plot ever existed. Like a soap bubble that vanishes with the touch of a hand, the “censorship–industrial complex” belongs to that mystical category of things that disappear when you examine them too closely. The failure to produce evidence is not for lack of trying. During the Biden administration, MAGA allies and politicians filed multiple lawsuits with the goal of exposing alleged censorship. None has done so. One of them, brought by the Missouri attorney general, made it all the way to the Supreme Court before justices asked for underlying evidence that the government had censored anyone. The answer was no. Another, brought against the Stanford research project by America First Legal—Stephen Miller’s team—failed in July, when a judge found the suit had no standing, no jurisdiction, and, after a discovery process requested by the plaintiffs, no evidence. There was no proof, in other words, that the Stanford research had resulted in anyone being censored. Other cases against the Biden administration were simply settled by President Trump’s Department of Justice without finding any evidence of “censorship” either. [ Renée DiResta: My encounter with the fantasy–industrial complex ] Now the Trump administration’s most dedicated ideologues have also failed, spectacularly, to prove the existence of a “censorship–industrial complex” inside the State Department. After months of searching, Beattie’s successor as undersecretary for public diplomacy, Sarah Rogers, recently decided to publicize the unimpressive results of the inquiry into the Global Engagement Center. But instead of writing a report admitting that the documents that surfaced contained nothing of interest, she leaked them, selectively, to an internet troll known as DataRepublican. Here is where the story becomes especially convoluted, and I will simplify as best I can. “DataRepublican” is the X pseudonym of Jennica Pounds, who has a history of misreading data and connecting dots to describe nonexistent conspiracies. But the plan went wrong: Upon receipt of raw documents from Rogers, including screenshots without context, Pounds decided that Rogers was a “Deep State” operative and refused to release them. Subsequently, it emerged that Pounds herself has been secretly employed by the Pentagon, which presumably makes her a deep-state operative too. But that’s another story. Because Pounds would not publish the documents, Rogers did so herself, in a long thread on X. As she must have known, they contained no evidence of conspiracy, no proof that anyone in the Biden administration censored millions or even dozens of social-media posts. Instead, Rogers, who is theoretically responsible for promoting good relations with people in foreign countries, went after a series of U.S. citizens. She found a GEC official who had about a dozen email exchanges with the Stanford project, almost all about Russian accounts. She posted a brief excerpt of the congressional testimony of Daniel Kimmage, a former State Department employee and GEC deputy coordinator, who truthfully explained that the center was set up to deal with foreign disinformation, not American media. Rogers wrote that “that was a lie,” without offering proof. Rogers also included several misleading posts about the Stanford project, plucking a number from a table and implying that it meant the researchers had somehow targeted more than 400,000 tweets, when they in fact had merely noted their existence. More to the point, the Stanford team did so after the election , not in some kind of smoke-filled room but in an academic report that is still publicly available and that DiResta has cited repeatedly. Rogers also criticized another very public, not remotely secret report, written jointly by the United States, Britain, Canada, Germany, Slovakia, and the European Union, investigating “gendered disinformation,” a subject that sounds very “woke” until you realize that deepfake porn videos and orchestrated misogyny are tactics regularly used against female politicians such as Annalena Baerbock, a former German foreign minister, or Giorgia Meloni, the Italian prime minister. The Iranian regime uses them to harass female dissidents around the world. Democratic governments would be negligent if they did not try to understand them. But even if you are not bothered by the online harassment of women in politics, it’s still impossible to argue that the publication of a report (and its translation into nine languages) proves the existence of a secret censorship–industrial complex stifling Americans’ views. “Watergate it was not,” Orna Blum, a former State Department official, wrote last week. [ Anne Applebaum: America surrenders in the information wars ] And if the scandal wasn’t Watergate, Rogers is not Bob Woodward. She is a public servant who dumped raw data online, seemingly without asking whether anyone would be damaged or which American foreign-policy interests could be served, all in the name of proving nothing. In the normal course of things the saga of the GEC documents would be, and should be, dismissed as a storm in a teapot. But unfortunately, the administration’s pursuit of a nonexistent censorship–industrial complex has already had real consequences for real people. In April 2025, Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced that he was closing the Global Engagement Center because it had “spent millions of dollars to actively silence and censor the voices of Americans they were supposed to be serving.” This was untrue, and even at the time there was no evidence for such an extraordinary statement. On the contrary, the GEC was the only institution in the U.S. government that was publicly tracking hostile international information operations, including by exposing websites in Africa or Latin America that appeared local but were in fact run by Moscow or Beijing. Rubio’s statement maligned the people who worked on these reports. Will the secretary of state now apologize to them? Compensate them? Rehire them? The closing of the center also means that no one is now doing that work. Thanks to Rogers, Beattie, and a handful of others, the U.S. decided to blind itself to the reality that Russia, China, and Iran, with its viral animated Lego videos , all run deceptive campaigns that reach millions of people around the world. And now Americans do nothing to halt, explain, or counter them. But it is not only American foreign policy that has been damaged. Following a series of expensive lawsuits as well as public harassment, Stanford shut down its internet-monitoring projects too. DiResta, one of the most prominent scholars in the field, left the university and was subjected to years of online harassment, an experience she has previously described in The Atlantic . Other research projects across the country also suffered, as funders and university provosts were, paradoxically, scared away by the Trump administration’s threats to curtail their free speech in the name of halting “censorship.” The study of foreign online campaigns and the proliferation of conspiracy theories has now become difficult and controversial, for people both inside and outside the government. That doesn’t mean that these campaigns don’t exist. It just means that Americans don’t know about them, don’t understand them, and cannot track them. As if this same conspiracy theory had not done enough damage, Rogers and others at the State Department are also putting the nonexistent censorship–industrial complex at the center of American foreign policy toward Europe now too. At a conference at the Hudson Institute last spring, Rogers said that a “censorship class” had already “scuttled to Europe” to pursue a supposed vendetta against Americans from across the ocean. At the same event, Senator Eric Schmitt of Missouri—who, in his previous role as the state’s attorney general, had brought one of the failed lawsuits against the Biden administration and supported legal challenges to the 2020 election—declared that “we are witnessing a deeply troubling assault on free speech” in Europe. [ Conor Friedersdorf: Europe’s free-speech problem ] These views, all of which derive from the same set of false stories, are actively shaping American policy in Europe. Late last month, the State Department put forth plans to spend $4 million to support right-wing media in Europe, including a consortium of “independent journalists” who would support the Trump administration’s view of the world. In recent months, the U.S. has imposed visa restrictions on Thierry Breton, a former EU commissioner who is now a private citizen, for his role in creating the Digital Services Act, a European law designed to protect minors, provide transparency around algorithms and targeted advertising, and ensure that behavior on the internet conforms to existing legislation. The U.S. also sanctioned four European researchers who campaigned for the digital-services law or against hate speech—essentially punishing them for their free speech, in the name of promoting free speech. Two of them, the leaders of a German organization called HateAid, called the visa ban “an act of repression by a government that is increasingly disregarding the rule of law and trying to silence its critics by any means necessary.” Belatedly, even some part of the Trump administration appears to have quietly concluded that all of this has gone too far and that maybe, in fact, it would be useful for the U.S. government to understand how hostile governments seek to manipulate the internet. In May, the State Department put out a tender for software developers who could help analyze “foreign adversarial propaganda” and thus replicate the work once done by the Global Engagement Center. In August, a State Department contractor also posted a job opening for research analysts who can, among other things, “evaluate how foreign governments, state-sponsored organizations, terrorist groups, and other malign actors use social media and digital communications to influence public opinion and targeted audiences.” As DiResta wrote this week, “they’re hiring people to do the very job they just spent 16 months claiming was a conspiracy.” So much time, energy, and money was wasted pursuing a fiction. Now more time, energy, and money will need to be spent to clean up the damage. This article originally misidentified Stanford as a target of a lawsuit brought by Missouri against the Biden administration.

title: New numbers show odds spike for major Bay Area earthquake in next 30 years
content: The risk of a large earthquake in the Bay Area has just been recalculated, and the odds have gone up, according to a recalibrated prediction from the U.S. Geological Survey. New federal numbers put the odds of a magnitude 6.7 quake or stronger in the Bay Area during the next 30 years at 74% — up from 72% in 2014 at the time of the previous prediction. These updated predictions were first reported by the San Francisco Chronicle, which requested updated data from the USGS. “It’s reinforcing what we already know,” United States Geological Survey geophysicist Kevin Milner said. “That we have to be prepared for a major earthquake. It is going to happen in most of our lifetimes.” Milner co-authored the first study and conducted the new one as well. He said the more time that passes without a major quake, the higher the probability of having one. Stanford University Aug 25 Earthquake sensors could help improve hurricane forecasts, Stanford scientists say East Bay Aug 13 Experts say the East Bay's Hayward Fault is ‘overdue' for a major earthquake The Hayward-Rodgers Creek Fault System, which stretches from San Jose to the San Pablo Bay, still has the highest probability of the Bay Area faults of producing a magnitude 6.7 or stronger earthquake at 34%. But the biggest increase is on the San Andreas Fault, which the USGS placed at 25.5%, which is up 3.6% from 2014. The San Andreas Fault stretches from Southern California through the Bay Area and north toward Eureka. It also produced the devastating 1906 earthquake, as well as the Loma Prieta quake in 1989. As the earthquake risk rises, so does the potential for damage — especially to critical infrastructure. Victor Zayas, president of Earthquake Protection Systems, said while building standards have made major advances, more protections are needed. “If we build any buildings, especially any new hospitals, we should be building them to not be damaged by earthquakes, not just not collapse,” Zayas said. USGS is working on developing new models to better understand earthquakes and their risks.

title: This dime sold for $1.2 million. The story behind its extraordinary value
content: With its darkened silver surface and coppery-gold hues, the more than 130-year-old dime may not look especially remarkable at first glance. But the 1894-S Barber dime is considered one of the rarest coins in American numismatics. On Sept. 1, one example sold for $1,250,500 at auction , more than 260 times the amount a teenage collector paid for it nearly seven decades ago. That collector was Q. David Bowers, who purchased the coin for $4,750 at age 19 in 1957. The headline-grabbing purchase helped launch what would become a prominent career in the rare-coin world, but the story behind the dime stretches back much further. The coin’s value comes largely from its rarity. Minted in San Francisco in 1894, the dime was produced during a period of economic hardship following the Panic of 1893, when demand for newly minted currency had declined sharply. As a result, the San Francisco Mint struck just 24 of the coins in June 1894. Today, only nine examples are confirmed to exist, though experts believe others may have survived. Because so few are known, and many remain in private collections for years or even decades, opportunities to buy one are exceptionally rare. scams Sep 2 Scams in the U.S. are at a record high. Yet most victims get no help and some end up losing even more Food & Drink Apr 25 Save money on your grocery bill with this simple food storage method “The mere mention of this coin is enough to attract the attention of even casual collectors,” auction house Stack’s Bowers said, describing the 1894-S as one of the classic rarities in coin collecting. Bowers recognized the coin’s significance when it came up for auction in 1957 with an estimated value of $5,000. He ultimately purchased it for $4,750, a sum that drew national attention at the time. “In 1957, I paid the record price of $4,750 for a beautiful uncirculated 1894-S dime,” Bowers wrote in a 2015 column for Coin World . He later sold the coin for $6,000, though its value continued to rise dramatically over the following decades. Before this year’s sale, only five 1894-S Barber dimes had appeared at auction since 2005, according to Stack’s Bowers. Those coins sold for between $1.3 million and $2.16 million. The example once owned by Bowers had not appeared at auction in 36 years. It previously sold for $77,000 in 1987 and $93,500 in 1990. This year, it returned to the auction block with an estimated value of $1.5 million. On Sept. 1, the coin sold for $1,250,500, adding another chapter to the story of one of the rarest dimes ever produced. This story was originally reported in Spanish for Telemundo .

title: Deleted email details alleged Trump-targeting push inside Letitia James’ office: ‘Find and pursue crimes’
content: A New York prosecutor accused state Attorney General Letitia James’ office of directing employees to "find and pursue crimes" involving President Donald Trump and entities tied to him, according to a report. The allegation stems from an email sent by Assistant Attorney General Daniel Wiesenfeld, who works in the Investor Protection Bureau of the New York Office of the Attorney General, which is led by Shamiso Maswoswe, the Times Union reported. The email was allegedly later wiped from the office’s servers, according to the outlet, while James’ office dismissed the matter as a personnel issue and rejected claims that the office was targeting people based on political beliefs. Wiesenfeld alleged that Maswoswe directed him to target "Trump himself, Truth Social, Hewlett Packard (DOJ approved merger)… without having a credible reason for targeting [these] organizations and individuals," according to the Times Union. Maswoswe previously worked as a trial attorney in the Justice Department’s Public Integrity Section from January 2016 until her termination in December 2017, under Trump's first term. In February 2021, she filed a discrimination lawsuit against the Justice Department, alleging she was unfairly terminated and subjected to discrimination based on her race, pregnancy and caregiving responsibilities. TRUMP'S LAWYERS PUT DEM AG ON NOTICE FOR TARGETING HIS FAMILY IN NY FRAUD FIGHT: 'CANNOT STAND' Wiesenfeld reportedly sent an agency-wide email to colleagues Friday with instructions "to find and pursue crimes committed by specific individuals and organizations affiliated with Donald Trump," the Times Union reported. The email reportedly was then allegedly wiped from servers, with a subsequent email sent from James' general counsel, Kumiki Gibson, informing employees that it was an "internal" matter and no employees were "in danger," the Times Union reported. "This is a personnel matter. The Office of the Attorney General is committed to upholding New York’s laws and protecting the rights and freedoms of all New Yorkers, regardless of political beliefs. We strongly reject any assertion to the contrary," a spokesperson for the Office of the New York Attorney General told Fox News Digital. The New York Post reported Wiesenfeld was placed on paid administrative leave. "This is more proof of the weaponization of the justice system by Letitia James to target President Trump and her political opponents. The far-left Democrats lawfare against President Trump, his family, and allies must stop," White House spokesperson Lauren Bis told Fox News Digital. Before Maswoswe joined James’ office in February 2022, she filed a discrimination suit against the DOJ. LETITIA JAMES HAMMERED AFTER NY MEDICAID FRAUD UNIT FUNDING FROZEN OVER INEFFECTIVE ENFORCEMENT She filed a complaint in February 2021 alleging she was unfairly fired during the Trump administration in 2017 and discriminated against for being Black and having a child. Maswoswe accused the DOJ of race discrimination due to her Zimbabwean descent and was scrutinized over her pregnancy, breastfeeding and caregiving responsibilities – seeking reinstatement, back pay and damages, according to court docs. In 2023, the two parties reached a settlement with Maswoswe, awarding her $795,000 to resolve all claims related to her employment and lawsuit. DOJ expressly denied that Maswoswe’s claim were true and the agreement says the payment was a compromise of disputed claims – not an admission that discrimination or retaliation occurred. James has been a longtime critic and legal adversary of Trump, launching a civil fraud lawsuit against him and the Trump Organization in 2022 after campaigning on investigating his business practices. The case initially resulted in more than $450 million in penalties, though an appeals court later upheld Trump’s liability while voiding the financial penalty.

title: GOP’s best hope is for Trump to shut up and go away: Republican leader
content: President Donald Trump and his many outbursts are becoming perhaps the biggest political liability for Republicans as the midterms approach, with one ex-RNC chief writing for The Hill that the party's best hope to survive would be for him to pipe down and get away from cameras. A veteran of the Reagan administration , Kevin Igoe previously served as deputy chief of staff of the Republican National Committee, as well as an executive director of the Maryland Republican Party. In a new op-ed for The Hill published on Wednesday, he admitted that "Republicans are in serious trouble" right now, and argued that the "one constant in this worsening picture is President Trump’s dominance of the Republican messaging machine." "I know my MAGA diehard friends are going to say that Trump is the best messenger ever," Igoe wrote. "That is true — if you are willing to settle for 33 percent of the electorate . If you actually want to win an election that is a referendum on Trump’s presidency, I suggest you get him off camera and take his phone away." He added: "Trump’s incessant comments about issues voters do not care about [are] an anchor around the neck of Republicans running in anything resembling a competitive district or state. Webster’s could define whiplash as an injury inflicted on anyone who attempts to follow Trump’s weekly policy reversals." Igoe further implored Republicans, including those in the MAGA sphere, to admit that "Trump’s gut does not rule the world." The president, he argued, "has reverted to his days as a developer," becoming obsessed with construction and renovation projects wherein "progress is defined as moving dirt." Meanwhile, voters' ideas about progress are defined by their ability to afford their lives week after week, something Trump has repeatedly brushed off as a non-issue. "Please recall these Trumpisms," Igoe wrote. First, President Trump has dismissed affordability issues as a ' hoax ' perpetrated by Democrats and said, ' this is the golden age of America .' He said the USS Lincoln was not deployed long enough in spite of documented supply and morale problems on board. He said Iran no longer had 'any spotters,' 'anti-aircraft' or “'radar' — until they shot down two American jets two days later. He then unilaterally claimed the Strait of Hormuz as 'American territory .'" He concluded: "My prescription to help Republicans salvage at least a tie in the Senate in the upcoming midterms is for President Trump to sit down, talk a lot less and stay off camera. You and I both know that is never going to happen — not now, and not in 2028. As we approach 2028, that will be a problem for Vice President JD Vance. At least now, he will not be surprised by what is to come."

title: US prosecutors refuse to say if they secretly obtained Don Lemon’s phone records
content: Experts have expressed deep concerns that the practice runs afoul of the fourth amendment’s right to privacy Federal prosecutors have declined to say whether they secretly obtained phone records for the journalist Don Lemon using an unusual administrative summons, his lawyers said in a Monday court filing , highlighting concern about a controversial legal authority the government has claimed to gather information as it charged Lemon and dozens of others with civil rights crimes in connection to a January protest at a church in Saint Paul, Minnesota. In January, officials served Verizon with an administrative summons for a log of Lemon’s phone records between 19 December and 20 January. The subpoena did not come from a grand jury, as is typical in criminal investigations, and also was not a court-approved search warrant. Instead, it was a unilateral request from the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), which said it was requesting the information under 19 USC 1509 – an obscure law that gives the department power to investigate records related to customs issues. Experts say the government is abusing that authority to gather records on journalists, activists, unions, non-profits and online critics, and have expressed deep concerns that the practice runs afoul of the fourth amendment’s right to privacy. title: The $1 Trump coins are here. Why spending them is legal but tricky
content: The U.S. Mint began selling $1 Trump coins Wednesday. Why it matters: The Trump coin sits in a rare middle ground: The Mint is promoting it as a collectible, but under federal law, it has a face value of $1 and can be used as real money. Driving the news: The U.S. Mint says the Trump coins are now "in circulation, so check your pocket change." The coins can be purchased in 25-coin rolls for $61 and 100-coin bags for $154.50. The U.S. Mint's website says the coins have "circulating finishes but have never been placed into circulation. However, they may be still used as legal tender." The big picture: Trump's coin has raised legal questions over whether a sitting president can appear on U.S. money. Why the Trump coin is "legal tender" "Legal tender" refers to U.S. money that can pay debts, taxes, dues and public charges, according to federal law . The U.S. Mint deems the $1 Trump coin legal tender with a face value of $1, regardless of what a collector pays for it. Yes, but: Legal tender doesn't guarantee every store will accept Trump coins. Federal law generally lets private businesses decide what forms of payment they'll accept. Americans have been reluctant to spend $1 coins. The Sacagawea dollar from the early 2000s struggled despite a multimillion-dollar marketing campaign, and the government stopped circulating presidential $1 coins in 2011 due to low demand. Debate over Trump coin as currency Catch up quick: Since the Trump coin was announced, questions have emerged about its design and legality because some federal laws restrict living people's portraits on U.S. coins. The Presidential $1 Coin Act of 2005 permits only $1 coins honoring deceased presidents issued under that presidential series and the Circulating Collectible Coin Redesign Act of 2020 prohibits any portraits of living people on the "tails" side of a coin. The other side: The Treasury Department argued in October 2025 that the coin can be made because the CCCRA does allow for "designs emblematic of the United States semiquincentennial." In July, a Treasury spokesperson pointed Axios to an Independent article reporting that the U.S. Mint had researched whether developing the coin would violate the law. Case in point: Calvin Coolidge, the 30th president, appeared alongside George Washington on a 1926 half-dollar celebrating America's 150th anniversary. The law authorizing the coin specifically said it "shall be legal tender in any payment to the amount of their face value." Although they sold for $1 apiece, their value was 50 cents. The bottom line: The Trump $1 coin is real money, but that doesn't mean it can be spent everywhere. Go deeper: 5 changes Trump could make to U.S. currency

title: Speculation rages as McConnell’s absence reaches shocking 'milestone'
content: Sen. Mitch McConnell's (R-Kentucky) last public appearance in the U.S. Senate was on June 11, when he took part in a roll call vote. And according to the Daily Beast, Wednesday, September 2 marks a "disturbing new milestone" for the 84-year-old GOP senator : "80 days since he was rushed to the hospital on June 14" and "nearly a month since the Republican's team last provided an update on his recovery." A long list of political figures, from conservatives to Democratic Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear, have been sounding the alarm about McConnell's extended absence from the Senate — arguing that his office needs to be much more transparent about his health. Daily Beast reporters Sarah Ewall-Wice and Farrah Tomazin note that McConnell's "prolonged vanishing act fueled rampant speculation and sparked outrage among critics." "The extraordinary cover-up has become the talk of Congress, with confusion growing over why the veteran lawmaker has insisted on keeping his Kentucky constituents and his party in the dark," Ewall-Wice and Tomazin explain. "He's been missing roughly the same number of days the House has been in session for the entire year. And this is at a time when Republicans are holding onto a narrow majority in the Senate, where every vote counts." The Daily Beast reporters add, "The former Republican Senate leader has already missed 60 votes in Congress since his hospitalization, on everything from a war powers resolution on Iran and policies on housing affordability, to the confirmation of new Attorney General Todd Blanche." According to a statement from McConnell's office, the 84-year-old senator was released from a rehabilitation center on August 6. But Ewall-Wice and Tomazin stress that "his team has offered no new information about how the senator is doing since then." "While the Senate has been in recess since August 8," the Beast reporters explain, "McConnell's office has not said if he will return with his colleagues when they arrive back in Washington in just under two weeks. Ahead of the 80-day mark of his disappearance from public view, his office also did not respond to the Daily Beast's questions about his recovery or how he's been spending his days. However, the Daily Beast visited his Washington, D.C., residence this week and observed a security detail — three unmarked SUVs with tinted windows — parked outside his home, along with two marked Capitol Police cars and officers at each end of his street." Ewall-Wice and Tomazin continue, "Most of the curtains in the house were drawn, although a first-floor window was open — and there was no mail piled up outside, as there had been when McConnell was in hospital prior to his release. The last image of McConnell was released by his team more than a month ago on July 27. It remains one of just two similar images released by his office since he vanished from public view more than two months ago."

title: Invisible coup: Shadow-docket decision just handed Trump Congress' power
content: Law school professor and Supreme Court analyst Leah Litman is warning that the Supreme Court's decision about the construction of the White House ballroom reflects a serious misunderstanding of the Constitution's separation of powers. Writing for The Atlantic on Wednesday, Litman explained that the problem is not that the federal courts temporarily blocked the project. Instead, it's that the president allegedly used taxpayer money for a White House construction project without authorization from Congress. Trump announced in 2025 that he would build the ballroom using full donations and that was why he didn't need to ask for permission from Congress. Then he failed to raise enough money to pay for new structure. Under the Constitution, Congress has the "power of the purse," dictating all spending authority over not merely the federal government but also over federal property, including the White House. Litman contends that the Court treated “the federal government” as if it were synonymous with the president, overlooking Congress’s separate constitutional role. The unsigned shadow-docket decision from the high court called the ballroom something that "the federal government" started. It's not accurate, Litman argued. Trump’s executive branch initiated the work, and Congress never authorized it. It's all part of the "unitary-executive theory and the accompanying expansion of executive power" that the Supreme Court has supported previously. "This theory maintains that all executive power resides in the president, and that Congress cannot limit the president’s exercise of that power," wrote Litman. "Yet these days, the president, occasionally with the Court’s blessing, is claiming to possess legislative powers too. That is the case when the president declines to spend funds that Congress has obligated or when the president decides to spend funds that Congress has not authorized. Under the Constitution, Congress, not the president, has the power of the purse. Nevertheless, the unitary-executive theory unites all government power in the president, paving the way for an executive unbound by law." When the Supreme Court tried to claim the lower courts all made a mistake, they tried to use the "doctrine of standing, which maintains that a plaintiff challenging the government’s actions must show that they have been injured by the actions they are contesting." The National Trust for Historic Preservation challenged the demolition and construction, alleging violations of federal law and a lack of congressional approval. It challenged the standing, but said that the building could continue while the matter worked its way through the courts. Broadway lawyer Michael C. Dorf penned his own column attacking the Supreme Court's "standing" argument, made the doctrine all the more difficult for citizens and organizations to meet. The far-right justices held that a historic-preservation advocate’s interest in seeing the White House before its East Wing was altered wasn't enough for a lawsuit. Chief Justice John Roberts and the Court’s three Democratic appointees dissented, saying precedent dictates that people can suffer legal harm even when the government's action impairs something they have a particularized professional, aesthetic, or personal interest in observing. The idea that an individual must "use" a place to have standing makes no sense for historic structures, whose central value is often visual, cultural, and symbolic, Dorf said. Litman argued that these "standing" requirements could make congressional statutes effectively unenforceable. If neither affected citizens nor preservation organizations can challenge allegedly unlawful executive action, it may be unclear who can enforce the legal limits Congress has enacted, she explained. Her final point was the argument that somehow Trump would suffer “irreparable harm” if lower courts blocked the project. Stopping potentially illegal conduct can't logically count as "injuring the president." Litman compared the ballroom case with another recent shadow docket decision, like the birthright citizenship case. Both matters are clearly outlined in the Constitution, but the Supreme Court's attempt to shield Trump's actions from judicial review while diminishing Congress’s ability to make enforceable laws doesn't hold water, she asserted.

The Port is also looking at the future. “The Port sees this plaza as step one in plans to continue to invest in seismic resilience and public space regeneration here at wharf this is a plaza a place that respects the wharf’s history while creating new space for what comes next,” Executive Director Port of San Francisco Michael Martin said.

title: Trump Admin Tells Court: Let OpenAI Rip Off The Intercept’s Articles
content: President Donald Trump’s Justice Department took the side of tech giant OpenAI in its court battle with The Intercept and other media companies over the company’s use of others’ creative work to train its artificial intelligence tools. In a federal court filing in New York, the Justice Department argued that the U.S. has a vested interest in OpenAI having access to a vast array of intellectual property. The Trump administration warned that restricting OpenAI’s access to the data could hamper scientific progress and harm the country’s dominance in the race for artificial intelligence. “The United States has a strong interest in continuing to develop a robust and competitive artificial intelligence industry that sets the standard for the practice and procedure of AI use globally,” said the filing, which was signed by associate attorneys general Stanley Woodward Jr. and Brett Shumate, along with the attorney general’s senior counsel Michael Weisbuch. Matt Topic, the litigating attorney representing The Intercept in its lawsuit, warned that the Trump administration’s position was out of touch and a threat to the financial survival of media outlets. “This is pretty reflective of the administration’s pro-AI policies, which are out of step with the public skepticism of AI and out of step with our long tradition in this country of protecting human expression,” said Topic. “If the administration’s position was accepted, it would result in an unprecedented, uncompensated transfer of IP rights from news organizations to tech companies.” “If the administration’s position was accepted, it would result in an unprecedented, uncompensated transfer of IP rights from news organizations to tech companies.” The Intercept originally filed its lawsuit against OpenAI and its partner Microsoft in February 2024, arguing that OpenAI’s use of work reported and written by its journalists constituted a breach of copyright law. In November 2024, the judge then presiding over the case dismissed all of The Intercept’s claims against Microsoft, but allowed its claim against OpenAI to proceed under the Digital Millennium Copyright Act. The Intercept’s case was later consolidated under U.S. District Judge Sidney Stein alongside a number of other media plaintiffs, including the New York Times, Tribune Media Company, and Ziff Davis. OpenAI has argued that its practice of hoovering up staggering amounts of copyright-protected materials to feed its large language models — the underlying technology powering generative AI tools like ChatGPT — falls under the domain of “fair use,” a doctrine protecting the unlicensed use of copyrighted material under certain circumstances. In its filing, the Justice Department supported OpenAI’s fair-use defense, accusing the Times and other plaintiffs of taking an overly narrow definition of the doctrine. OpenAI’s use of the material, the government argued, met the criteria for “transformative” use, one of the ways in which “fair use” comes into play. “In this litigation, the New York Times seeks to narrow fair-use doctrine to exclude the training of OpenAI’s large language models (LLMs). That result would be inconsistent with basic copyright law principles and severely hamper ‘the Progress of Science and useful Arts,’” the filing says. “An erroneous fair use ruling would hamper competition in the market for LLMs, because only the largest technology companies might have the capital necessary to pay licensing fees.” Related OpenAI on Surveillance and Autonomous Killings: You’re Going to Have to Trust Us The filing is the latest move from the Trump administration to protect the interests of U.S.-based artificial intelligence companies amid an AI arms race with companies based in other countries, most notably China . In December 2025, Trump signed an executive order aimed at creating a federal standard, applicable in all 50 states, to “ensure that the United States wins the AI race, as we must.” Topic, The Intercept’s attorney, said this position — combined with the fact that the Justice Department has not been privy to any discovery in the case — shows that the Trump administration is operating from a fixed position in support of tech companies, rather than arguing the merits of the case. “What they’re saying isn’t based on any understanding of actual facts,” Topic said. “It just reflects what Microsoft’s and OpenAI’s PR machines have been putting out into the public.” The post Trump Admin Tells Court: Let OpenAI Rip Off The Intercept’s Articles appeared first on The Intercept .

title: Abdul El-Sayed dubbed ‘veteran’ by Soros-linked propaganda newspaper distributed in Michigan
content: DETROIT — A propaganda newspaper that once accepted a massive grant from George Soros’ Open Society Foundation falsely described beleaguered leftist Michigan U.S. Senate candidate, Abdul El-Sayed as a veteran, according to a copy of that paper obtained by Fox News Digital. " El-Sayed — veteran, doctor, and former health official — is Democratic Senate pick," reads a headline in the August 2026 edition of The Michigan Independent. The papers were distributed in Michigan, and photos of the headline made the rounds on social media last week. The breadth of the paper's circulation is unclear, but Fox News Digital obtained a physical copy in Michigan. LIZ PEEK: MICHIGAN CAN STOP THE SOCIALIST FEVER RAGE — OR WATCH IT SWALLOW THE SENATE The purportedly independent paper circulating in Michigan has a Washington, D.C. non-profit's name and address — The American Independent Foundation at 800 Maine Ave SW — emblazoned in the bottom left corner of the front cover. As it turns out, the papers aren't independent at all. TOP MEDIA OUTLETS FAIL TO DISCLOSE WHO IS BANKROLLING THEIR AI REPORTERS In 2024, The American Independent Foundation, a 501(c)(3) tax-exempt organization, received a $500,000 grant from George Soros' Foundation to Promote Open Society, according to that organization's IRS 990 disclosure form . Soros, a billionaire businessman, investor and philanthropist, is a renowned leftist mega donor known for his support of progressive and Democratic causes. The Washington Free Beacon first reported the Soros connection. The content of the Michigan Independent story mentions nothing of El-Sayed being a veteran, nor does it clarify that while El-Sayed holds an M.D., he has never been a physician. El-Sayed's campaign forcefully condemned the publication's classification of the candidate. "Abdul has never claimed to be a veteran, he never would out of his respect for those who served, and any outlet or group writing about our campaign should do their homework and not allow this to happen again," spokesman Cole Wozniak told Fox News Digital. The American Independent did not return Fox News Digital's request for comment. JONATHAN TURLEY: FAKE POLLSTER'S STUNT WAS A RECKLESS GAME WITH REAL RACES Twelve other state-based newspapers are part of the network Soros helped fund, including papers in key swing states like Ohio, Pennsylvania, Wisconsin, Virginia and others that have become increasingly important in the 2026 midterms due to competitive U.S. Senate races, including Maine and Alaska. Some of the outlets share the same featured stories. At the time of this writing, both The Ohio Independent and The Pennsylvania Independent feature a story titled "Report: Trump and Big Oil see financial windfall as Americans pay more at pump". SOROS NETWORK REBUILDS PROGRESSIVE PROSECUTOR PUSH AFTER STRING OF ELECTION LOSSES An associated 501(c)(4) political activism organization, American Independent Media, is also affiliated with the network of news outlets. Each state-based website says it is a project of American Independent Media whose mission is "to use journalism to educate the public, giving them the information they need about local and federal issues." David Brock, founder of the far-left media watchdog Media Matters and a high-profile Democratic operative, is also connected to the shadowy network of papers. He is the founder of the 501(c)(3) American Bridge , also a titan in left-wing politics. American Bridge's 501(c)(4) arm, the AB Foundation, donated $23.5 million to American Independent Media in 2024. DEM SENATE HOPEFUL’S ‘PHYSICIAN’ CAMPAIGN PITCH UNDER FIRE AFTER LICENSE RECORDS REVEAL KEY GAPS The story about El-Sayed was penned by Alyssa Burr, whose LinkedIn page says she's the Michigan Politics Reporter at The American Independent. She previously worked at MLive Media Group, which publishes prominent state newspaper Michigan Live, and before that, the New York Times .

title: Police chief in Mississippi town where 1-year-old was killed has been fired
content: Senatobia, where white officer shot and killed Kohen Wiley, terminates chief who reportedly used racist slurs in texts Late Tuesday, the city of Senatobia, Mississippi fired its police chief, Harold Vanderford, after it was reported that Vanderford regularly used racist slurs against Black people in his text messages. The town, which is about 40% Black , made national news earlier this year after a white officer fatally shot and killed Kohen Wiley , a one-year-old Black baby, while responding to a shoplifting call at Walmart. Officers fired into a vehicle, shooting the driver and killing the toddler, who was being held in his mother’s arms. Though Vanderford submitted a resignation letter earlier on 1 September, the city’s board of aldermen unanimously voted to reject it and to terminate the officer instead. Vanderford’s firing came just under a week after the city wrote in a statement that, despite the messages, he would “continue to serve the City with the confidence that was placed in him at the time that he was appointed as Chief”.
